dataset.name: BrainActive P3 High Ability Pilot
dataset.disclaimer: Original reasoning-practice items inspired by the BrainActive curriculum research (MOE 2026 HAL context, CogAT, UK 11+ NVR/VR, Singapore thinking-skills & heuristics). Not affiliated with or predictive of any MOE or GEP assessment. Not a mock exam.
dataset.design: v0.4 is a RESEARCH-DERIVED LEARNING JOURNEY. Questions are grouped into Skill-Practice progressions where the same skill develops Explore (accessible) -> Think (multi-step) -> Challenge (complex) -> Master (non-routine, integrates strategies). Difficulty rises via rule complexity, constraints and near-miss distractors, NOT bigger numbers or harder words. Each item carries thinking_skill + why_level so the learning intention is explicit. 8 v0.3 items were rewritten; Tier-1 gaps 6.6 (Pattern Application) and 3x3 matrices were added; a Master-tier integrate item was added. v0.4.1: defect-fix delta from the frozen content QA. 6 items corrected (0046, 0025, 0043, 0027, 0048, 0047); progression architecture and the other 44 questions unchanged.
dataset.level_model: Explore / Think / Challenge / Master. 'difficulty' field uses the same level names.
dataset.gates: No DB, no renderer, no production app code, no 100+ generation. Content review only.

questions.question: Find the next number: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ___?
questions.explanation: Gaps: +1, +2, +3, +4, +5. Each gap grows by 1, so the next gap is +6: 16 + 6 = 22.
questions.thinking_skill: Spotting a changing (second-order) difference.
questions.why_level: Explore: a single clear rule; builds the habit of looking at differences between terms, not just the terms.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Explore anchor of the 1.1 progression).

questions.question: Find the next number: 3, 6, 5, 12, 7, 24, 9, ___?
questions.explanation: Two woven sequences. Odd positions: 3, 5, 7, 9 (+2). Even positions: 6, 12, 24 (x2). The missing 8th term is the next even-position term: 24 x 2 = 48.
questions.thinking_skill: Splitting two interleaved sequences.
questions.why_level: Think: two rules must be held in mind at once; the first real multi-track reasoning in the 1.1 path.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Think step of 1.1).

questions.question: Find the next number: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, ___?
questions.explanation: Each term is the previous term multiplied by a growing integer: x2, x3, x4, x5. Next is x6: 120 x 6 = 720.
questions.thinking_skill: Detecting a scaling (non-additive) multiplier rule.
questions.why_level: Challenge: the rule is not additive and numbers grow fast; the child must test 'multiply by an increasing integer' rather than a fixed operation.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (extends 1.1 to its Challenge ceiling).

questions.question: 4 is to 7 as 5 is to ___? (Find the relationship in the first pair, then use it.)
questions.explanation: Relationship: +3. 4 + 3 = 7, so 5 + 3 = 8.
questions.thinking_skill: Inferring a single-operation relation and applying it.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: one obvious operation; teaches the analogy format before compound rules.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore anchor for 1.2).

questions.question: 2 is to 5 as 4 is to ___? (The rule is not a simple round multiplier.)
questions.explanation: Rule: x2 then +1. 2 -> 5; so 4 -> (4x2)+1 = 9. Distractors use x2 (8) and off-by-one (10, 11).
questions.thinking_skill: Inferring and testing a two-part rule (x2 then +1).
questions.why_level: Think (rewrite of v0.3 0003): the relation is not a round multiplier, so the child must hypothesise and test a compound rule - HA-appropriate, not a rote x4.
questions.source_inspiration: Rewrite of v0.3 0003 per audit (x4 was too transparent).

questions.question: A triangle and a square together weigh 11. A square and a circle together weigh 13. A triangle and a circle together weigh 10. Which shape is heaviest?
questions.explanation: Add the three: each shape counted twice = 34, so one of each = 17. Circle = 17-11 = 6, square = 17-10 = 7, triangle = 17-13 = 4. The square (7) is heaviest.
questions.thinking_skill: Solving a small system by combining equations.
questions.why_level: Think: must combine three pair-weights; multi-step but concrete.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Think step of 1.3).

questions.question: A, B and C are single digits. A + B = 10, B + C = 8, and A + C = 6. What is A?
questions.explanation: Try digits: if A = 4 then B = 6 (A+B=10) and C = 2 (B+C=8); check A+C = 4+2 = 6. Works, so A = 4.
questions.thinking_skill: Solving a 3-unknown system (guess & check / sum-and-subtract).
questions.why_level: Challenge: more unknowns; rewards systematic checking rather than a single insight.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Challenge step of 1.3).

questions.question: Ben has 2 more marbles than Ali. Ali has 5 marbles. Who has the most?
questions.explanation: Ali = 5, so Ben = 5 + 2 = 7. Ben has the most.
questions.thinking_skill: Translating 'more than' into a comparison.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: one comparison step; introduces quantitative comparison before chained cases.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore anchor for 1.4).

questions.question: Ali has 3 more marbles than Bob. Bob has 2 fewer than Chen. Chen has 10. Who has the most?
questions.thinking_skill: Chaining several comparisons into a full order.
questions.why_level: Think: three linked comparisons; the child must build the whole order, not just one step.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Think step of 1.4).

questions.question: Tom is taller than Sam. Sam is taller than Lee. Who is the shortest?
questions.explanation: Taller order: Tom > Sam > Lee, so Lee is shortest.
questions.thinking_skill: Building a linear order from two transitive clues.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: two clues read directly; introduces ordering before merged partial orders.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore anchor for 2.1).

questions.question: Four teams race. Red finishes before Blue. Green finishes after Yellow. Blue finishes before Green. Yellow finishes before Red. Order them from fastest to slowest.
questions.explanation: From the clues: Yellow < Red < Blue (Yellow before Red, Red before Blue). Also Blue < Green and Yellow < Green. Together: Yellow < Red < Blue < Green. Fastest to slowest: Yellow, Red, Blue, Green.
questions.thinking_skill: Merging two partial orderings into one total order.
questions.why_level: Think (rewrite of v0.3 0007): the clues do not form a single read-off chain; the child must merge separate partial orders - a real deduction, not a list to recite.
questions.source_inspiration: Rewrite of v0.3 0007 per audit (original was a read-off chain).

questions.question: Anya, Ben and Cai sit in a row of three. Anya is in the middle. Ben is not at the left end. Who sits at the left end?
questions.explanation: Anya is in the middle (seat 2). Left (1) and right (3) are Ben and Cai. Ben is not left, so Ben is right and Cai is left.
questions.thinking_skill: Placing a fixed person, then applying a negative constraint.
questions.why_level: Think: one fixed position plus one negative constraint; the core constraint-matching move.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Think step of 2.2).

questions.question: Four friends each do a different activity: swimming, cycling, running, skating. (1) Ben cycles. (2) Cindy runs. (3) Amy does not swim. (4) Dan does not skate. Who swims?
questions.explanation: Ben cycles and Cindy runs, leaving swimming and skating for Amy and Dan. Amy does not swim, so Amy skates and Dan swims. Check clue 4: Dan does not skate - true, he swims. Consistent.
questions.thinking_skill: Multi-clue assignment (constraint satisfaction).
questions.why_level: Challenge: four entities, four attributes, several clues; a table helps - the ceiling of 2.2.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Challenge step of 2.2; the v0.3 logic bug was fixed before v0.4).

questions.question: If it is sunny, the cat sits by the window. The cat is NOT by the window. What can we conclude?
questions.explanation: Rule: sunny -> cat by window. Cat NOT by window, so it cannot be sunny. You cannot tell where the cat is, only that it is not sunny.
questions.thinking_skill: Using the contrapositive (must-be-true from a negation).
questions.why_level: Think: requires reversing the implication; the classic HA logical move.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Think step of 2.3).

questions.question: If it rains, the match is cancelled. If the match is cancelled, the picnic moves indoors. It is raining. What MUST be true?
questions.explanation: It rains -> match cancelled -> picnic indoors. So the picnic must be indoors. The others contradict the chain.
questions.thinking_skill: Chaining two conditional rules (transitive if-then).
questions.why_level: Challenge: two linked rules; the conclusion must be carried through both steps, not just one.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Challenge step for 2.3).

questions.question: Which is the odd one out? A red square   B red triangle   C blue square   D red square
questions.explanation: Three of the four are red (A, B, D). C is the only blue one, so by the majority property (colour) C is the odd one out. Shape alone is a trap (B is the only triangle).
questions.thinking_skill: Finding the property that three share (majority dimension).
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: introduces odd-one-out by checking which attribute 3 share, not just any difference.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore anchor for 2.4).

questions.question: Four figures: A red square, B red square, C red square, D blue square. Which does not belong, and why?

options.text: D (it is the only blue one)

questions.explanation: Three figures share BOTH shape (square) and colour (red). D is also a square but is blue, so the distinguishing dimension is colour: D is the odd one. Option D is a trap (there is no triangle).
questions.thinking_skill: Attending to two dimensions to find the true odd-one-out.
questions.why_level: Think (rewrite of v0.3 0010): a single-dimension guess (shape) fails; the child must check both shape and colour - higher ceiling than 'curved vs straight'.
questions.source_inspiration: Rewrite of v0.3 0010 per audit (curved-vs-straight was too low-ceiling).

questions.question: All squares are blue. All blue things are small. Which MUST be true?
questions.explanation: Every square is blue, and everything blue is small, so every square is small. The others reverse the direction of the rules and need not be true.
questions.thinking_skill: Chaining set inclusions (transitive).
questions.why_level: Challenge: must chain inclusions without reversing them; a genuine deductive trap.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the single 2.5 item).

questions.question: Dog is to bark as cat is to ___?
questions.explanation: Relation: animal : the sound it makes. Dog barks, cat meows.
questions.thinking_skill: Identifying a familiar relation (sound).
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: a clear relation; teaches the analogy format before less obvious pairings.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore anchor for 3.1).

questions.question: Pen is to write as knife is to ___?
questions.explanation: Relation: tool : the action it is used for. A pen is used to write; a knife is used to cut.
questions.thinking_skill: Mapping a tool-to-action relation (less cliche than body parts).
questions.why_level: Think (rewrite of v0.3 0013): replaces the over-used bird:wing example with a tool-action pair that still requires finding the relation, not recalling a stock phrase.
questions.source_inspiration: Rewrite of v0.3 0013 per audit (bird:wing was a cliche IQ item).

questions.question: Which word is different? A dig   B shovel   C spoon   D rake
questions.explanation: Shovel, spoon and rake are tools (things). Dig is the action of using a tool, so it is different.
questions.thinking_skill: Separating nouns (things) from actions.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: a simple semantic split; a gentle verbal warm-up.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the single 3.2 item).

questions.question: In a code, each letter becomes the next letter (A->B, B->C, ...). How is CAT written?
questions.explanation: Shift each letter forward one: C->D, A->B, T->U = DBU.
questions.thinking_skill: Applying a simple letter shift.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: a single +1 shift on a short word; introduces coding before decoding.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore anchor for 3.3).

questions.question: In a code, each letter means the next letter (A means B, ...). The code word is DPEF. What real word does it stand for?
questions.explanation: Each code letter is one step ahead, so decode by shifting back one: D->C, P->O, E->D, F->E = CODE.
questions.thinking_skill: Reversing a letter shift to decode.
questions.why_level: Think: decode (reverse the shift); deterministic and generatable.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Think step of 3.3).

questions.question: Mei reads every Saturday. She also reads whenever it rains. Today she is NOT reading. What MUST be true?

options.text: It is not Saturday and not raining

questions.explanation: She reads if Saturday OR raining. Today she does NOT read, so neither condition holds: it is not Saturday and it is not raining. B and C would make her read; D adds info we are not given.
questions.thinking_skill: Must-be-true from the negation of a combined condition (contrapositive of an OR).
questions.why_level: Think (rewrite of v0.3 0016, re-levelled from a mis-labelled Challenge): requires applying negation across two conditions - a real HA inference, not a trivial read.
questions.source_inspiration: Rewrite of v0.3 0016 per audit (was a trivial modus ponens mis-levelled as Challenge).

questions.question: An L-shape has its corner at the top-left. It is rotated 90 degrees clockwise. Where is the corner now?
questions.explanation: Rotating 90 degrees clockwise moves the top-left corner to the top-right corner. Because the shape is asymmetric (an L), the orientation actually matters.
questions.thinking_skill: Mentally rotating an asymmetric shape.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: one 90-degree turn of an L; orientation matters, unlike a symmetric dot.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore anchor for 4.1).

questions.question: An arrow points up. It is rotated 90 degrees clockwise, then another 90 degrees clockwise. Which way does it point now?
questions.explanation: Up -> right (first turn) -> down (second turn). Two 90-degree clockwise turns = 180 degrees, so the arrow points down.
questions.thinking_skill: Tracking rotation across two steps.
questions.why_level: Think (rewrite of v0.3 0017): must accumulate TWO turns, not read a single labelled corner; the orientation must be held in mind.
questions.source_inspiration: Rewrite of v0.3 0017 per audit (single corner-dot turn was minimal).

questions.question: The letter 'b' is reflected in a vertical mirror (left-right flip). Which letter does the reflection look like?
questions.explanation: A vertical (left-right) mirror flips 'b' so its round part moves to the right, making it look like 'd'.
questions.thinking_skill: Mirror reflection across a vertical axis.
questions.why_level: Think: a vertical mirror reverses left and right; Tier-1 spatial.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the single 4.2 item).

questions.question: A cube has a star on the FRONT, a dot on the TOP, and a circle on the RIGHT. Which face is opposite the star?
questions.explanation: Front, top and right are three faces meeting at one corner. The face opposite the front is the back. (Top is opposite bottom; right is opposite left.)
questions.thinking_skill: Identifying the face opposite a given face on a cube.
questions.why_level: Think: must place three adjacent faces and infer the opposite; a step before full net-folding.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Think step for 4.3).

questions.question: A cube net: centre square Y, with W above Y, V below Y, X left of Y, Z right of Y, and U below V (V and U form a column under Y). Folded with Y as the front face, which square is the BACK face (opposite the front)?
questions.explanation: Fold Y as front: X=left, Z=right, W=top, V=bottom, and the remaining square U folds to the back. The face opposite front (Y) is the back = U.
questions.thinking_skill: Folding a net to find the opposite face.
questions.why_level: Challenge: unfold/refold mentally; the Tier-1 spatial ceiling.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Challenge step of 4.3).

questions.question: A cube has a dot on its TOP face and a star on its FRONT face. You rotate it 90 degrees to the right around the vertical axis. Where is the star now?
questions.explanation: Rotating around the vertical axis to the right turns the front face to the right side. The top face (dot) stays on top. The star moves from front to right.
questions.thinking_skill: 3D rotation around the vertical axis.
questions.why_level: Challenge: side faces move while top stays; hard spatial reasoning, a research-flagged area.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the single 4.4 item).

questions.question: Each step the shape gains one side AND its colour alternates red, blue, red... A red triangle becomes a blue square, then a red pentagon. What comes next?
questions.explanation: Two rules: sides go 3,4,5 so next is 6 (hexagon); colour goes red, blue, red, so next is blue. The next shape is a blue hexagon.
questions.thinking_skill: Continuing a two-feature transformation.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: two clear rules running together; builds feature-tracking.

visual_spec.rule: add one side AND alternate colour red/blue

questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the single 4.6 item).

questions.question: A big square has a small triangle attached to its LEFT side and a small circle attached to its RIGHT side. Which option matches this combined figure?

options.text: triangle on the left, circle on the right
circle on the left, triangle on the right
triangle on top, circle on bottom
two circles, one on each side

questions.explanation: The figure joins a triangle on the left of the square and a circle on the right. Option A matches; B swaps the sides, C and D place the shapes wrongly.
questions.thinking_skill: Composing a figure from two placed parts (spatial assembly).
questions.why_level: Think (rewritten in v0.4.1 to be a genuine combining-shapes task: the child must attach two parts at the correct positions, not just recognise a described house).

visual_spec.result: square with triangle left and circle right

questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the single 4.7 item).

questions.question: An arrow points up, then right, then down (turning 90 degrees clockwise each step). What does it point to next?
questions.explanation: The arrow goes up -> right -> down. One more 90-degree clockwise turn points it left.
questions.thinking_skill: Continuing a single-rule rotation sequence.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: three steps shown, predict the fourth; one rule only.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore anchor for 5.1).

questions.question: An arrow rotates 90 degrees clockwise each step and its colour alternates red, blue, red... Step 1: up red. Step 2: right blue. Step 3: down red. Step 4: left blue. Step 5: up red. At Step 7, what are its direction and colour?
questions.explanation: Direction cycles every 4 steps: step 7 = step 3 = down. Colour alternates red(odd)/blue(even); step 7 is odd so red. At step 7: down, red.
questions.thinking_skill: Predicting a later term using a cycle plus a second alternating attribute.
questions.why_level: Think (rewrite of v0.3 0022): must use the cycle modulus AND track a second feature; not a recite-the-cycle.

visual_spec.rule: clockwise 90 per step + colour alternate red/blue

questions.source_inspiration: Rewrite of v0.3 0022 per audit (4-step cycle returning to 'up' had no real prediction).

questions.question: Top-left is a circle. Top-right is a circle with a dot. Bottom-left is a square. Following the same change (add a dot), what should the bottom-right be?
questions.explanation: Change from top-left to top-right is 'add a dot'. Apply the same change to bottom-left (square): square -> square with a dot.
questions.thinking_skill: Mapping a transformation across a 2x2 matrix.
questions.why_level: Think: find the rule in row 1, apply to row 2; Tier-1 figural reasoning.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Think step of 5.2).

questions.question: Complete the 3x3 matrix. Rule DOWN each COLUMN: add one dot (1 dot -> 2 dots -> 3 dots). Rule ACROSS each ROW: colour changes red -> blue -> green. Top-left is a red circle with 1 dot. The bottom-right cell is ___?
questions.explanation: Down column 3 the dots go 1 -> 2 -> 3. Across row 3 the colour goes red -> blue -> green. So bottom-right = green circle with 3 dots.
questions.thinking_skill: Completing a 3x3 matrix with two simultaneous rules (row and column).
questions.why_level: Challenge (3x3 matrix; row/column rule directions corrected in v0.4.1): two rules apply at once - the "wow" visual item research flagged as important.

visual_spec.col_rule: add one dot down the column
visual_spec.row_rule: colour changes red->blue->green across the row

questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (addresses audit MISSING: only a 2x2 matrix existed; research wants 3x3).

questions.question: Four figures: A triangle with 1 dot, B triangle with 2 dots, C square with 3 dots, D triangle with 4 dots. Which does not belong?
questions.explanation: A, B and D are triangles (only dot count changes). C is the only square, so it does not belong by shape.
questions.thinking_skill: SPONCS odd-one-out by shape.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: one shape differs; introduces figural classification.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the single 5.3 item).

questions.question: A small square changes into a large square (size only changes). Using the same change, a small circle changes into a ___?
questions.explanation: The change is 'increase size'; the shape stays the same. Small square -> large square, so small circle -> large circle.
questions.thinking_skill: Mapping a single feature (size) in a figure analogy.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: one mapped feature; teaches figure-analogy format before dual features.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore anchor for 5.4).

questions.question: A small red square changes into a large blue square (size flips AND colour flips, shape stays). Using the same change, a small blue circle changes into a ___?
questions.explanation: Two changes: size small->large, and colour flips (red->blue, so blue->red). Shape stays the same. So small blue circle -> large red circle.
questions.thinking_skill: Mapping two transformations at once (size + colour).
questions.why_level: Think (rewritten in v0.4.1): the colour flip is now a reversible red<->blue rule shown by the example, so the child can legitimately infer blue->red; maps two features, shape constant.

visual_spec.rule: flip size AND flip colour (red<->blue), keep shape

questions.source_inspiration: Rewrite of v0.3 0025 per audit (single-feature mapping was too elementary).

questions.question: Groups of dots: 2, then 3, then 5, then 8, then 13. How many dots come next?
questions.explanation: Each group has as many dots as the two previous groups combined: 2+3=5, 3+5=8, 5+8=13, so 8+13=21.
questions.thinking_skill: Continuing a sum-of-previous-two progression.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold: an approachable, recognisable pattern.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the single 5.5 item).

questions.question: A number plus 5 equals 12. What is the number?
questions.explanation: Work backwards: the result was 12, so before adding 5 the number was 12 - 5 = 7.
questions.thinking_skill: Reversing a single operation.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold for the Working-Backwards progression: one reverse step; introduces the heuristic.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore step of 6.1).

questions.question: A number is doubled, then 3 is added, and the result is 15. What was the starting number?
questions.explanation: Work backwards: the result was 15, so before adding 3 it was 12, and before doubling it was 12 / 2 = 6. Starting number = 6.
questions.thinking_skill: Reversing two operations in the correct order.
questions.why_level: Think: undo the steps backwards (the core WB move); the middle of the 6.1 progression.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Think step of 6.1).

questions.question: A bus had some children. At a stop, 8 got off and 5 got on. Now there are 14 children on the bus. How many were on the bus at first?
questions.explanation: Work backwards from 14: before 5 got on there were 14 - 5 = 9; before 8 got off there were 9 + 8 = 17. So 17 at first.
questions.thinking_skill: Working backwards through a real-world context.
questions.why_level: Challenge: unfamiliar framing; must reverse two changes in a story, not just numbers.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Challenge step of 6.1).

questions.question: A number is doubled, then 4 is added, then 5 is subtracted, and the result is 11. What was the starting number? Check your answer by going forward.
questions.explanation: Work backwards: 11 + 5 = 16; 16 - 4 = 12; 12 / 2 = 6. Check forward: 6 x 2 = 12, +4 = 16, -5 = 11. Correct, so start = 6.
questions.thinking_skill: Working backwards through a 3-step process AND verifying with the forward check (combining two heuristics).
questions.why_level: Master: non-routine; the familiar single algorithm does not apply directly - the child must reverse a 3-step process and confirm via guess-&-check/verification. (Corrected in v0.4.1: the middle "=20" step was inconsistent; the process is now double -> +4 -> -5 = 11.)
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Master step of 6.1; combines working-backwards with verification).

questions.question: Some coins are 2-dollar and some are 5-dollar. There are 7 coins in total and they make 23 dollars. How many 5-dollar coins are there?
questions.explanation: Try 3 five-dollar coins (=15) and 4 two-dollar coins (=8). Total value 23 and total coins 7. That fits, so 3 five-dollar coins. (Systematic guess-&-check across the few cases.)
questions.thinking_skill: Systematic trial across a few cases.
questions.why_level: Explore scaffold for Guess-&-Check (adjusted in v0.4.1 to need a little more checking than the original 3-coin version, while staying P3-accessible).
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (Explore step of 6.2).

questions.question: There are some 2-dollar and 5-dollar coins. There are 6 coins in total and they make 18 dollars. How many 5-dollar coins are there?
questions.explanation: Try 2 five-dollar coins (=10) and 4 two-dollar coins (=8). Total value 18 and total coins 6. That fits, so there are 2 five-dollar coins.
questions.thinking_skill: Guess-&-check across more combinations, systematically.
questions.why_level: Think: more combinations to test in order; the main 6.2 step.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the Think step of 6.2).

questions.question: Amy has 5 more stickers than Ben. Amy gives Ben 2 stickers. Now who has more stickers, and by how many?
questions.explanation: Originally Amy leads by 5. When Amy gives Ben 2, Amy loses 2 and Ben gains 2, so the gap shrinks by 4 (5 - 4 = 1). Amy still has 1 more.
questions.thinking_skill: Constant-difference under a transfer.
questions.why_level: Think: a transfer of 2 reduces the difference by 2+2 = 4; a distinct Singapore heuristic.
questions.source_inspiration: Carried from v0.3 (re-evaluated: retains as the single 6.3 item).

questions.question: A machine uses this rule: 1 -> 4,  2 -> 7,  3 -> 10. What should 8 become?
questions.explanation: Each output is the input x 3 + 1: 1->4, 2->7, 3->10. So 8 -> 8 x 3 + 1 = 25. Distractors: x3 only (24), x3-2 (22), x3+4 (28).
questions.thinking_skill: Discovering a rule, then applying it to a new (far) case.
questions.why_level: Explore (rewritten in v0.4.1 to add transfer: the child must find x3+1 and apply it to 8, not just count weekdays).
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (addresses audit MISSING: Tier-1 6.6 Pattern Application was absent).

questions.skill: apply a repeating rule to a far term
questions.question: A row of tiles repeats: red, blue, red, blue, red... (1st, 3rd, 5th are red). What colour is the 12th tile, and what colour is the 13th?
questions.explanation: Odd positions are red, even positions are blue. 12 is even -> blue; 13 is odd -> red.
questions.thinking_skill: Using a discovered repeating rule to predict a far term (application, not just next-step).
questions.why_level: Think (fills MISSING 6.6): must apply the rule to a position far along, not merely continue - the real Pattern-Application skill.
questions.source_inspiration: New in v0.4 (addresses audit MISSING: 6.6 Pattern Application).

questions.question: Each step the shape rotates 90 degrees clockwise AND gains one side. Step 1: triangle (3 sides) pointing up. Step 2: square (4) pointing right. Step 3: pentagon (5) pointing down. What is Step 4?
questions.explanation: Two rules combine: rotate 90 CW (up->right->down->left) and add one side (3->4->5->6). Step 4 = hexagon (6 sides) pointing left.
questions.thinking_skill: Integrating two rules (rotation + shape change) to predict a non-routine step.
questions.why_level: Master (genuine non-routine item): the familiar single algorithm does not apply; the child must hold BOTH rules and combine them - the integration ceiling.
